name: Angelo Vermeulen
half:
Angelo Vermeulen has not advised any theses in this repository. Their own contributions to the repository consist of 11 articles, with the latest item dated 2026. Their research interests are heavily concentrated in arts and creative practice, which appears in eight of their items. Other research areas include futures and philosophy (3), climate and disaster (2), culture and identity (2), environment and sustainability (1), online and distance learning (1), and language and literacy (1).

Based on their published work, their research focus often involves the intersection of art, science, and technology. They have explored themes such as the integration of art into transdisciplinary sustainability research, the use of speculative design to examine climate change and the space race, and the role of immersive installations in reshaping bodily self-perception. Their work also addresses postcolonial perspectives on translating art-science installations between Western contexts and the Global South, as well as the use of biological research as a metaphor for human ideology. Additionally, they have investigated the intersection of biological mortality and lifelike technologies, and the potential for community art projects to address biodiversity. Their research has also touched upon the use of blended learning approaches that combine online learning with on-site new media art practice.

Angelo Vermeulen has not advised any theses in this repository. Their presence in the repository is limited to 11 articles, with the most recent item dated 2026. Based on their published work, their research focus is heavily centered on the intersection of arts and creative practice, which accounts for 8 of their items. They also engage with futures and philosophy (3), climate and disaster (2), culture and identity (2), environment and sustainability (1), online and distance learning (1), and language and literacy (1).

Their research frequently utilizes art as a tool for transdisciplinary inquiry and speculative exploration. They have explored how collaborative art can facilitate idea generation within sustainability research, as seen in their work on Biomodd. This project also serves as a case study for integrating online learning with on-site new media art practice through a blended learning approach. Their work often bridges the gap between scientific concepts and artistic expression, such as using biological research as a metaphor to investigate human ideology in space or examining the tension between biological mortality and advancing lifelike technologies.

Vermeulen’s work explores complex themes including degrowth, finitude, and the implications of biological engineering. They have investigated the disconnect between technoscientific predictive models and the lived experiences of populations affected by climate change through speculative proposals like the Multispecies Roundtable for Climate Impact. Their research also touches upon postcolonial perspectives, specifically regarding the translation of art-science installations from Western contexts to the Global South.

In terms of specific thematic areas, they have explored bodily self-perception through immersive installations using auditory and vibrotactile stimuli. They have also engaged with themes of cultural immortality and the tension between human desire and biological necessity in extreme environments, such as space settlement. Their involvement in the BUKAS Lab suggests an interest in fostering pluridisciplinary initiatives at the intersection of art, design, technology, and futures literacy, particularly within the context of socioeconomic justice and sustainable development. While they have not supervised any students within this specific repository, their body of work demonstrates a consistent pattern of using creative practice to address philosophical, environmental, and technological questions. Evidence regarding their specific capacity for thesis supervision is thin, as no student supervision is recorded in this database.

Angelo Vermeulen has not advised any theses in this repository. Their own contributions to the repository consist of 11 articles, with the most recent item dated 2026. Their research output spans a wide range of sub-topics, with a primary focus on arts and creative practice, which appears in 8 of their items. Other areas of interest include futures and philosophy (3), climate and disaster (2), culture and identity (2), environment and sustainability (1), online and distance learning (1), and language and literacy (1).

Their work frequently explores the intersection of art, science, and technology. For example, they have examined how collaborative art can facilitate idea generation within transdisciplinary sustainability research through the Biomodd project. This work has also been analyzed from a postcolonial perspective regarding the translation of art-science installations from Western contexts to the Global South. Their research into the BUKAS Lab focuses on artscience exploration and futures literacy within the Global South, aiming to foster pluridisciplinary initiatives at the intersection of art, design, technology, and socioeconomic justice.

Vermeulen also investigates themes of mortality and technology, such as the intersection of biological mortality and advancing lifelike technologies in the context of death, degrowth, and finitude. Their work explores the tension between human desires for cultural immortality and the biological necessity of adaptation in extreme environments, specifically through projects like Ēngines of Ēternity which uses biological research as a metaphor to investigate human ideology in space. Other speculative and artistic inquiries include exploring the tension between climate change and the space race through somatic experiences and interactive performance, as well as addressing the disconnect between technoscientific predictive models and the lived experiences of populations affected by climate change through speculative proposals for multispecies roundtables. Additionally, they have explored immersive installations designed to reimagine bodily self-perception through auditory and vibrotactile stimuli, and community art projects such as the Biodiversity Tower. Their research also touches upon the integration of online learning with on-site new media art practice. While their research covers diverse topics ranging from space settlement ideology to community-based public art, the central thread remains the use of artistic inquiry to engage with complex scientific, social, and philosophical questions. Evidence of their specific thesis supervision patterns, such as the number of students advised or the specific topics they have guided, is not available in this repository as they have not advised any theses here.
